Tokenized stocks are turning into a distribution business.

Putting a stock onchain has become straightforward. Most issuers buy the underlying shares through a broker and mint tokens against them, which leaves buyers choosing between tokens that offer near-identical exposure. Whoever gets those tokens in front of the most investors pulls ahead.

Exchanges start that race with an advantage because their traders are already there. Binance's bStocks and Kraken's xStocks are two of the three largest platforms, and together with Ondo they hold most of the wrapped stock market.

Being listed everywhere only helps if the token is cheap to trade. Investors will pick whichever version gets them the best price.

The issuers that win will pair the widest reach with the deepest markets.

every investment/trade I give to my agent would become an experience.

what did we think would happen? what actually happened? what did we get wrong?

next time we find a similar investment, retrieve it and learn from it.

if my crypto agent misses a major token unlock I don’t just want it to remember:

mistake = a lesson = a new research rule = a new test to improve the agent.

finally I would build my own benchmark.

every time I change the system I want to know:

combine all six and you don’t really have an AI trading bot anymore.

Virtual Reality vs. Augmented Reality
$META vs. $SNAP

After Meta unveiled its new VR glasses, everybody started saying Snap’s Specs were finished. That makes no sense. They’re different products designed to do different things.

It’s like saying LeBron James will replace Messi as the greatest striker of all time. They play different sports.

Meta’s VR glasses take you into a virtual world. Snap’s Specs are designed to add digital information to the real world around you. Meta’s Ray-Ban Display glasses are another product again: they’re more practical today for simple things like messages, directions and translations, but they show information on a small display in one lens. Snap is trying to build a more immersive AR experience, where digital content appears in the space around you.

Imagine walking down the street and seeing directions in front of you. You point at a building and ask how much it costs to rent in the area. You see a guy wearing a suit you like, ask where to buy it, and get sent straight to the website. At the supermarket, you ask to see your shopping list. You order a cab by pointing to where you want it to stop. All of this without pulling out your phone or stopping.

That’s the potential of AR. It could make everyday life easier and slowly reduce our reliance on phones. Maybe one day the technology will be built into our eyes, like Black Mirror. We’re not there yet, but AR glasses are a step in that direction.

Snap’s Specs are still early, bulky and expensive. Meta is also working on more advanced AR technology. But Snap is aiming directly at the kind of AR future I believe in.

I believe AR is part of the future, and I believe in Snap’s social network. Each could be a home run, especially if $SNAP can find a deep pocket partner for AR. At a $7–8 billion valuation, $SNAP feels like a free option to me. It’s currently my largest position. $META and $SNAP are taking different approaches to the future of glasses.

When do you sell a stock? $WGS 

$WGS was trading around $80 when it reported earnings. The company said its average reimbursement per test was lower than expected as more patients shifted to whole genome testing.

The stock collapsed. I thought the market was treating this as a permanent problem. Whole genome testing gives you a more complete picture, yet insurers were reimbursing it at a lower rate than exome testing. I believed that gap could improve as coverage became more established.

When WGS fell below $40, I recommended backing up the truck. I put 30% of my own portfolio into it.

Slowly, the stock started climbing back toward $80. But as it moved from $80 toward $100, the story changed. At the lower price, we were assuming reimbursement would improve. At the higher price, the market was already beginning to price that improvement in. And full reimbursement for everything GeneDx is doing still wasn’t there. The stock may have run ahead of itself.

So, when do you sell? I don’t give people a sell price. If you have a five-year view, a 20% drop may not change the thesis. If you have a shorter timeline and the stock is up 140%, you may decide to take some profits. That’s up to you. I’ll explain why I buy a stock, but I’ll never tell you when to sell it because each person has a different time frame.

When software becomes a commodity, the moat is how much value you deliver per unit of compute.

Anyone can build the same features. Few can serve as many users, across as many use cases, without restrictive limits.

Model quality compounds that advantage: better results with less compute mean higher gross margins and more compute to train the next, more efficient model.

That’s the winning flywheel for the next 24 months.
